enrichment.short_title: Oral property compromise and section 2 formalities
key_facts: Mr Nwoko bought 31 Benares Road from his cousins the Nwezes in 2001 for an orally agreed £135,000 but with a written contract showing £105,000 to reduce stamp duty.

After partial payment disputes, the parties orally compromised in May 2002 that Mr Nwoko would sell the property at the best price and pay net proceeds to the Nwezes after discharging the Halifax mortgage.
Mr Nwoko later refused to proceed with the sale; the Recorder held the original oral sale agreement unenforceable under section 2 but ordered specific performance of the compromise.
On appeal the sole issue was whether the oral compromise was itself a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land within section 2.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on permission limited to whether an oral compromise requiring sale of property at best price was caught by section 2 of the 1989 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; oral compromise held not a contract for sale or disposition of land within section 2; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2 requires writing for contracts under which land or an interest in land is actually sold or disposed of between identified parties; an agreement obliging a vendor to market property and sell to a third party if a buyer is found is not within the section, even if specific performance may later compel a sale.
legal_issues: Whether an oral compromise to sell property at best price is a contract for sale of land under section 2
Meaning of 'for' in 'a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land'
Whether Jelson Ltd v Derby County Council supports the appellant's argument
Whether constructive trust or restitution alternatives survived the appeal

enrichment.short_title: Hand-arm vibration syndrome negligence at Llanwern
key_facts: Three former Llanwern steelworkers appealed after Judge Hickinbottom dismissed lead HAVS claims from a group of 57 similar cases.
Corus admitted breach of duty from 1976 for excessive vibration exposure but disputed a duty to reduce vibration levels and causation of sensorineural symptoms.
The judge found Corus should have surveyed tools, trained workers, warned them and provided medical surveillance but not that it had to reduce vibration exposure.
Each appellant suffered sensorineural Hand/Arm Vibration Syndrome symptoms from jackhammers and pneumatic tools over decades.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Cardiff County Court on duty to reduce vibration exposure and McGhee/Fairchild causation in lead HAVS test cases.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed on liability; judge should have found a duty to reduce vibration levels and that breach materially increased injury risk; claims remitted for damages assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Once excessive vibration exposure was established, the employer had to justify failing to reduce it; without evidence of impracticability the judge could not speculate on cost or industrial relations; failure to reduce exposure and provide training materially increased HAVS risk under McGhee and Fairchild.
legal_issues: Whether employers owed a duty to reduce vibration exposure levels
Whether breach of training and surveillance duties was causative
Application of McGhee v National Coal Board and Fairchild v Glenhaven
Whether warnings and medical surveillance failures were appealable given fact findings below

enrichment.short_title: Drug cash forfeiture and Article 6 expert adjournment
key_facts: Customs seized £39,990 in cash from Mr Lappin at Holyhead in October 2001 and magistrates later ordered forfeiture as drug-trafficking proceeds.
Forensic analysis showed cocaine contamination on sampled banknotes above typical circulation levels; the appellant's explanation for carrying the cash was rejected.
The Crown Court refused adjournments so the appellant could instruct an expert to challenge contamination evidence despite earlier case management directions.
The case stated asked whether refusing adjournment breached Article 6 by denying equality of arms on expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a case stated from the Crown Court following dismissal of an appeal against magistrates' forfeiture order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no breach of Article 6 in proceeding without defence expert evidence given the appellant's persistent failure to comply with directions.
enrichment.ratio: While civil forfeiture proceedings require a fair hearing, a party who repeatedly ignores timetables to instruct an expert cannot complain that refusal of a late adjournment was disproportionate or created inequality of arms.

enrichment.short_title: Clock House boundary hedge ownership appeal
key_facts: Mr Derwent destroyed a laurel hedge dividing Clock House (Mr Seeckts) from Linden House in May 2000, triggering long-running boundary litigation.
Ownership turned on construction of a 1968 conveyance plan with T-marks, dimensions and covenant references to existing hedges.
The trial judge declared Mr Seeckts owner of boundary features between points A-B-C-D and awarded £1,500 damages.
The Derwents appealed arguing dimensions on the plan should fix the boundary rather than T-marks indicating Clock House ownership of boundary features.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a trial on ownership of destroyed boundary vegetation and related boundary features.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on ownership; paragraph 2 of the order directing surveyors to fix the precise boundary line set aside as beyond the pleaded issues.
enrichment.ratio: Inward T-marks on a conveyance plan normally indicate boundary features belong to the burdened property; where a well-established laurel hedge existed, dimensions provide only a general indication and do not displace T-mark ownership; a judge cannot compel parties to agree a precise boundary line beyond the pleaded ownership issue.
legal_issues: Construction of the 1968 conveyance and plan 1724
Whether T-marks or dimensional measurements determine boundary ownership
Whether a laurel hedge was an existing boundary feature in 1968
Whether the judge could order parties to fix the precise boundary line

key_facts: Mr and Mrs O'Connor lost their assured tenancy at 1A Railway Mews after leaving for Ireland in 2000 and leaving Michael Walton to pay rent without informing Notting Hill Housing Trust.
Rent arrears led to a suspended possession order and eventual eviction in September 2002 when only £83 remained outstanding.
Kensington and Chelsea found them intentionally homeless; the county court dismissed their section 204 appeal.
They had arranged for Walton to occupy the flat but were unaware he failed to pay rent and concealed possession proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on points of law from a county court section 204 appeal against an intentional homelessness review decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; local authority decision quashed because section 191(2) good-faith ignorance of relevant facts was not addressed.
enrichment.ratio: Section 191(2) mitigates deliberate acts done in good faith while unaware of relevant facts and does not require ignorance to be reasonable; a review decision treating unreasonable failure to safeguard the tenancy as decisive without separately asking whether omissions were in ignorance of relevant facts misapplies the statute.

key_facts: The Secretary of State introduced a Harmondsworth fast-track pilot for single male asylum applicants from designated safe countries, building on the Oakington process.
Applicants could be interviewed the day after arrival with a decision on the third day and compressed appeal stages thereafter.
Refugee Legal Centre challenged the timetable as inherently unfair, seeking an extra day for instructions and post-interview representations.
Statistics showed very high refusal and appeal dismissal rates; solicitors reported tight timescales but few individual unfairness complaints.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the lawfulness of the Harmondsworth fast-track asylum procedure.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; Collins J held the scheme was not inherently unfair and its flexibility enabled fair processing in practice.
enrichment.ratio: A fast-track asylum system is not unlawful merely because timescales are tight if it remains flexible, provides legal representation, includes a full appeal right unlike Oakington certification, and lack of widespread representative complaints indicates the process is capable of fairness in operation.

enrichment.short_title: Associated companies and small companies tax relief
key_facts: Gascoines Group Ltd, Newark Cattle Market Company Ltd and Saracens Securities Ltd appealed Special Commissioners' decisions on entitlement to small companies relief.
The issue was whether Saracens was an associated company of Gascoines and Newark, reducing applicable profit thresholds.
Mr D W H Gascoine held 71% of Gascoines, Gascoines wholly owned Newark, and trustees of a settlement of which he was settlor held 99% of Saracens.
Attributed control under sections 416 and 417 meant all three companies were under Mr Gascoine's control.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on a preliminary issue from Special Commissioners determining associated company status for small companies relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Special Commissioners correctly held Saracens associated with Gascoines and Newark; bias challenge rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Under sections 13(4), 416 and 417 ICTA 1988, control includes attributed rights of associates such as trustees of a settlement where the individual is settlor; where the same person is taken to control multiple companies they are associated companies regardless of absence of factual day-to-day control.
